title: African theology
hook: John Mbiti: I am because we are, and the Christian God was already sought in Africa

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kosuke Koyama in the rice fields, and a God who walks. Your line was the speed of love. Who did you slow down for? Day one thousand two hundred eighty-four.

Ask who you are, and you'll probably give a name, a job, a town. Now ask it a different way: who are you with? John Mbiti grew up in Kenya hearing that question answered in the second way. He went abroad to study theology, read the great European books, and came home with a puzzle. Many of the books he'd been handed, as he saw it, started with the lonely individual: I think, I choose, I believe. The villages he knew started somewhere else, with family, with neighbors, with the ancestors and the children not yet born. A person was a thread in a cloth. Mbiti spent his life asking what the gospel sounds like when you start from the cloth. That question is today's word.
screen: `A PERSON IS A THREAD IN A CLOTH.`

segments.voice: Mbiti was an Anglican priest and a scholar, and he became one of the voices people mean when they say African theology. Two ideas of his travel far. The first is his summary of how, as he saw it, many African peoples understand a person: I am, because we are. The community makes the person, and the person belongs to the community. It flips the famous European line about thinking and existing. You aren't first a self who then joins a group. You become a self through the people who hold you. Second, the Bible has its own picture of this shape. Paul calls the church a body, and writes in the King James words: "whether one member suffer, all the members suffer with it; or one member be honoured, all the members rejoice with it." Pain is shared. Joy is shared. In Acts, the first believers "continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers." The Greek word behind fellowship there, koinonia, means sharing in common. Third, God was not a stranger. Mbiti gathered the ways African peoples had long spoken of God: creator, provider, the one who sees. He argued that missionaries did not carry God into Africa as if God had been absent. People had already been seeking, and the gospel came as an answer to a search already under way. Paul says something close in Athens: God made the nations so "that they should seek the Lord, if haply they might feel after him, and find him." Fourth, why it matters on an ordinary day. A faith that starts from we notices who's missing from the table.

Here's the practice: honor your community. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the people who made you who you are. A grandparent. A teacher. A neighbor who fed you. A friend from a hard year. Let them come one at a time, and for each one, say quietly inside: because you were, I am. If you pray, you can give thanks for them by name. If you don't, just notice how many hands are in your story. Then, if you like, think of someone for whom you are one of those hands. The bell holds the time.
African theology. In John Mbiti's hands, faith that starts from the we, and a God who was already being sought before any missionary arrived.
Your line: I am because we are. Today, thank one person out loud for a part they played in your life, even a small part, even years ago. Day one thousand two hundred eighty-four.

howItsDone: In African churches, as elsewhere, Christians pray for their families, neighbors and those who came before them by name, and gather to share both mourning and celebration as a community.

fork.setup: you're John Mbiti, home from studying abroad. the books you read start from the lonely I. your village starts from we. what do you do?
options: drop the village's way of seeing; the books are the real theology.
start from the we, and read the Bible again from there.
fork.reveal: Mbiti started from the community, and argued that the gospel came to people already seeking God. read beside him, scripture has its own picture: one body, fellowship.

original.note: Greek: fellowship, sharing in common. the word in Acts 2:42 for the first believers' life together.

notes: Mbiti's line 'I am, because we are; and since we are, therefore I am' (African Religions and Philosophy) is in copyright; it is spoken as his sentence but sources mark it as paraphrase (quoted: null). Confirm this is acceptable or reduce to the index carry only.
'How many African peoples understand a person' is Mbiti's own claim, attributed to him; confirm phrasing is attributed clearly enough.

Biography: Kenyan, Anglican priest, studied abroad; confirm. No dates given by design. The hook dramatizes his upbringing and his sense that European theology started from the individual; confirm fair.
'Flips the famous European line about thinking and existing' alludes to Descartes without naming him; confirm.
Mbiti's argument that God was known and sought in Africa before missionaries (Concepts of God in Africa) is summarized; confirm fair.
κοινωνία glossed as 'sharing in common'; standard lexicon sense, confirm.
